https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A "Price Comparison Report" produced through Michigan Bus Purchasing (Spec #23976) on July 17, 2025 for the Troy School District, comparing quotes from three dealers — Hoekstra, Holland, and Midwest Transit — for two 77-passenger electric school buses in the EV Conventional (2024-2025 Phase 2) category.

Headline pricing. Product base prices per bus are $385,980.00 (Hoekstra), $384,420.00 (Holland), and $393,081.00 (Midwest Transit). After chassis and body options, the configured price per bus is $411,968.00, $413,621.00, and $424,098.00 respectively. With dealer options added, Hoekstra's unit price rises to $414,105.00 while Holland ($413,621.00) and Midwest Transit ($424,098.00) are unchanged. For the two-bus order, the grand totals are $828,210.00 (Hoekstra), $827,242.00 (Holland), and $848,196.00 (Midwest Transit).

Specifications and warranties. Each bus includes a 246 KWH EV battery system, a minimum 23,000 lb rear axle, Electronic Stability Control air brakes, Bendix Intellipark electronic parking brakes, and an EV rear charging port with door (a $1,876.00 add for Hoekstra, standard for Holland, $6,288.00 for Midwest Transit). Warranty coverage includes a standard high-voltage battery warranty of 8 years/175,000 miles and towing coverage of 5 years/100,000 miles, plus a no-charge 5-year/100,000-mile extended body and chassis warranty listed among Hoekstra's dealer options.

Options detail. The report itemizes dozens of body options with per-vendor pricing or S/E (standard equipment), N/A, or N/C (no charge) notations — including competing air-conditioning systems (a Carrier AC-126K 124,000 BTU unit at $22,517.00 for Hoekstra, a Valeo REVO 130,000 BTU unit at $27,500.00 for Holland, and a Trans Air 120,000 BTU unit at $24,425.00 for Midwest Transit), interior wall color, crossing gate arms, emergency exit windows (increase from 2 to 4), floor covering, mid-body rear heaters, LED interior dome lights, adjustable and crossview/rearview mirror systems, noise-reduction perforated ceilings, roof paint, an AM/FM radio with PA system, air-ride driver's seats, fire-block seat deletions, and stop-arm signal configurations. Hoekstra's additional dealer options include an $850.00 back-up camera, Corashield underbody undercoating ($619.00), stainless steel manifold plumbing ($167.00), stainless steel radiator piping ($240.00), and an air entrance door in lieu of electric ($261.00).

Purpose. The comparison provides the pricing basis for the board's award decision on the two-bus purchase; the accompanying finance recommendation favors Hoekstra Transportation for its bus configuration and dealer-installed options.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Troy School District's Statement of Revenues and Expenditures for the fiscal year July 1, 2024 through June 30, 2025 (unaudited) reports budget-to-actual results across the General Fund, the Consolidated Debt Service Funds, and several special-revenue funds.

General Fund (101): Actual revenues were $192,866,818 against an approved budget of $194,857,883. By source, actual revenues were Local $46,908,178.58 (budget $46,923,373), State $129,164,531.94 (budget $130,300,126), Federal $3,985,000.62 (budget $4,442,113), and Interdistrict $12,809,107 (budget $13,192,272). Actual expenditures totaled $193,505,461 against a budget of $198,652,719. Minutes of the Troy School District Board of Education regular meeting held July 15, 2025 at the district Administration Building, 4400 Livernois. President Philippart called the meeting to order at 9:35 a.m. Present were board members Philippart, Alic, Anne, Haupt, Melton, and Potts, with Mrs. Zendler attending via remote communications. Also present were Superintendent Machesky; administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Montante, Trudel, and Pagel; and two members of the audience. There were no recognitions, no additions or deletions, and no public communication.

Consent agenda: On a motion by Mr. Haupt, supported by Mrs. Anne, the board approved items A through G by a 6-0 vote (Zendler absent/remote): minutes of the June 3, 2025 Special Board Meeting, June 3 Closed Session, and June 3 Board Workshop; minutes of the June 17, 2025 Board Meeting; the Treasurer's Report for May 2025; the Settlement Terms of Batista v Office of Retirement Services litigation; and rescheduling of the October 21 board meeting and the December 2 and January 6 board workshops.

Personnel: On a motion by Mrs. Anne, supported by Mrs. Alic (6-0), the board extended administrator contracts through June 30, 2026 (without tenure in the administrative positions, subject to the Administrative Handbook layoff provision). Those named include principals Vernon Burden (Athens High), Patrick Griffin (International Academy-East), Remo Roncone (Troy High), Ryan Brinks (Smith Middle), Jonathan Cross (Baker Middle), Anthony Morse (Boulan Park Middle), Brian Zawislak (Larson Middle), Michelle Barsh (Martell), Karen Bush (Barnard), Mike Cottone (Troy Union), Erin Detmer (Leonard), Tammy DiPonio (Costello), Scott Keen (Morse), Lindsay Keegan (Schroeder), Shari Pawlus (Hill), David Recker (Hamilton), Harleen Singh (Bemis), and Amy Wallace (Wattles); assistant principals Kerry Brennan, Melissa Curth, and Dan House (Troy High), Megan Henry (Athens), Gabrielle Naus (IA-East), Ross Burdette (Baker), Cassandra Conaton (Smith), Stephan Henning (Larson), and Kristy Pierce (Boulan Park); and directors/supervisors Rob Carson (Maintenance and Operations), Christine Foren (Special Education), Natalie Haezebrouck (Teaching & Learning), Erin Keyser (Early Childhood Program), and Troy Wissink (Technology).

On a separate motion by Mr. Haupt, supported by Mrs. Alic (6-0), the board extended through June 30, 2027 the contracts of the four assistant superintendents: Dan Trudel (Business Services), John Pagel (Employee Services), Kris Griffor (Elementary Instruction), and Christine DiPilato (Secondary Instruction).

Superintendent evaluation: The board reported it had recently completed Superintendent Dr. Richard Machesky's performance evaluation and shared the assessment publicly, rating him EXEMPLARY for meeting or exceeding expectations in all categories. The statement credits his execution of the district's strategic plan and 'LEARNING FOR ALL' vision; continued fiscal strength with sufficient fund balance to absorb state-funding disruptions; integration of a new business operations team; bond projects tracking at or below budget; alignment of a Multi-Tiered System of Support to address achievement gaps (particularly for special education, English Language Learners, and economically disadvantaged students); new secondary assessments; and math and literacy professional development for all grade levels.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A "Staffing Process Update" presented to the Troy Board of Education on September 2, 2025, describing the Troy School District (TSD) hiring process end to end and profiling the district's 2025 class of new hires.

Hiring process. The central office posts generalized openings to allow candidates to apply through TSD, the Oakland Consortium, Indeed, MSBO, and similar channels. Screening committees operate via Applicant Central and use candidate profile/stakeholder surveys, a structured screener interview, the Applitrack Teacher/Admin Fit Assessment, verification of certification and endorsement, general reference checks, and consistent questions geared to the candidate profile, with an emphasis on seeking diversity applicants when available. Building-level recruitment includes the TSD Elementary Teacher Job Fair, attendance at in-person and virtual university recruitment fairs, referral of top candidates to Applicant Central, and inviting top job-fair candidates to a day of TSD professional learning.

Interview committees, which include administrators and department and building representatives, look for evidence of profile characteristics, subject-matter knowledge, teaching qualities, a focus on students, and best practices. Candidates respond to a writing prompt and must complete a teaching or administrative observation, provide proof of certification and MTTC status where applicable, undergo thorough reference and background checks and fingerprinting, submit previous evaluations, and may complete other performance-based exercises. The committee recommends top candidate(s) for each opening. Candidate pools are organized by grade band — K–2 and 3–5 at elementary, and 6–8 and 9–12 by subject matter/specialty.

Approval chain. Finalists interview with the Assistant Superintendent/Director of Employee Services, the Assistant Superintendent of Elementary/Secondary, and the Superintendent, leading to determination of a contract offer and Board of Education final approval. The presentation also references an Administrator Hiring Rubric used to evaluate administrative candidates.

2025 class profile. The district hired 45 new TSD teachers, broken down as 3 preschool, 10 elementary, 17 secondary, and 15 special education. Of these, 7 are TSD graduates and 24 have educational experience beyond a bachelor's degree. The district also added 6 new TSD administrators and moved 2 existing TSD administrators into new roles, drawing from 3 internal and 3 external administrator candidates. The presentation closes with a questions-and-thank-you slide.

What it is
Agenda item 2.E (Recognition) at the September 16, 2025 Regular Meeting of the Troy Board of Education, a suggested resolution proclaiming September 2025 as National Suicide Prevention Month.

Background
The Oakland Community Health Network (OCHN) asked school boards throughout Oakland County to partner with it by approving this proclamation at their September board meetings.

Key points in the resolution
- September is National Suicide Prevention Month, intended to raise awareness of prevention resources.
- World Suicide Prevention Day is observed each year on September 10.
- Suicidal thoughts can affect anyone regardless of age, gender, race, orientation, income, religion, or background.
- Per the CDC, each year more than 48,000 people died by suicide.
- Suicide is the second-leading cause of death for people aged 10 to 34.
- References the National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI) and the 988 lifeline as crisis resources.
- OCHN is committed to being a Zero Suicide organization.

Resolution

Acceptance of the resolution, with a recorded Yes/No vote.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
At its Regular Meeting on September 16, 2025, the Troy Board of Education considered agenda item 2.E, a suggested resolution recognizing September 2025 as National Suicide Prevention Month. The item arose from a request by the Oakland Community Health Network (OCHN), which asked school boards throughout Oakland County to partner with it by approving such a proclamation at their September board meetings. The recommended action was acceptance of the resolution, with spaces for a mover, a supporter, and recorded Yes and No votes.

The resolution's WHEREAS clauses establish its rationale: September is known as National Suicide Prevention Month and is intended to help raise awareness of suicide prevention resources available in the community; World Suicide Prevention Day is observed each year on September 10; and suicidal thoughts can affect anyone regardless of age, gender, race, orientation, income level, religion, or background. It cites the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) statistic that each year more than 48,000 people died by suicide, and states that suicide is the second leading cause of death for people 10 to 34 years of age. The resolution notes that organizations such as the National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI) and the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline, 988, work to help individuals in crisis and to reduce stigma around the topic. It adds that every member of the community should understand that throughout life's struggles people need the occasional reminder that everyone is silently fighting their own battles, and that OCHN is committed to being a Zero Suicide organization that cultivates a network of providers engaged in the Zero Suicide philosophy.

The operative clause states that the Oakland Community Health Network hereby recognizes September 2025 as National Suicide Prevention Month, and calls upon individuals, government agencies, public and private institutions, businesses, faith-based organizations, and schools to recommit the state to increasing awareness and understanding of suicide prevention and the need for appropriate and accessible services to assist individuals in crisis. The document appears in the meeting's Recognition section (agenda item 2) and is presented for board adoption as a community-partnership proclamation rather than an action with fiscal impact.

What it is
A slide-deck recommendation from the Attendance Area Review Committee (AARC) presented at the September 16, 2025 Regular Meeting, proposing middle-school enrollment adjustments for Troy School District.

Goals
- Goal 1: Right-size middle schools with equal student ratios
- Goal 2: Resolve double splits
- Goal 3: No impact on high schools

Background
District practice reviews enrollment every 5-10 years; prior AARC groups convened in 2015 and 2018, and a 62-member Facilities Review Committee ran in 2021/22 to inform the 2022 bond. Current middle-school enrollment ranges 590-870; the new Smith Middle School is built for an optimal 750. A double split exists at Troy Union, with single splits at Smith, Baker, Wattles, and Hamilton. All four middle schools rank in Metro Parent's top 6 in Michigan.

Recommendation (updated Option C)
- No changes to existing boundaries
- All Troy Union students go to Smith
- Student-of-choice families primarily placed in elementary pathways feeding Smith and Baker (65 enrolled)
- Beginning Fall 2026, open enrollment to Larson closes except concurrently enrolled siblings (~20 students/year)
- Somerset Apartment students follow their elementary cohort to middle school and then Troy High (~190 impacted); new Somerset families in 26/27 enroll at Smith or Baker
- Smith, Baker, and Athens offer open enrollment

Timeline
2025/2026 prepare for adjustments; 2026/2027 changes implemented. Students in grades 5-8 in Fall 2025 (classes of 2029-2032) are not impacted and may stay in their current building; siblings kept together; advanced programming, curriculum, and athletics remain consistent across all four middle schools.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
An Attendance Area Review Committee (AARC) recommendation presentation for the Troy School District Board of Education, presented at the Regular Meeting of September 16, 2025. Its three stated goals are to right-size the middle schools with equal student ratios (Goal 1), resolve double splits (Goal 2), and produce no impact on the high schools (Goal 3).

Background and rationale: The district reviews enrollment patterns and challenges every 5-10 years, with previous AARC groups in 2015 and 2018, and a Facilities Review Committee of 62 members in 2021/22 that ran a 6-month process to create recommendations for the 2022 bond proposal with staff, student, cabinet, and Board feedback. The problem framing centers on enrollment 'splits' as students transition between levels — a double split at Troy Union and single splits at Smith, Baker, Wattles, and Hamilton — plus the goal of a world-class programmatic experience and balanced ratios. Middle-school building enrollment ranges from 590 to 870. Additional factors include enrollment projections, birth rate and students of choice (SOC), the new Smith Middle School built for an optimal enrollment of 750, and Metro Parent rankings placing all four middle schools in the top 6 in Michigan.

AARC Outcomes — Option C (updated after the committee concluded, based on questions the group raised) lists middle-school figures of Baker 616, Boulan Park 603, Larson 625, and Smith 682. Under this option all Troy Union students go to Smith; all students living in community housing follow their currently assigned elementary school to that school's assigned middle school; and Somerset Apartments (319 students, drawn from 6 elementary schools) would go to Boulan Park but would begin following their cohort to Boulan, Baker, or Smith.

Recommendation for BOE Approval: no changes to existing boundaries. SOC families will primarily be placed in elementary pathways that feed Smith and Baker where appropriate (65 enrolled). Beginning Fall 2026, open enrollment to Larson will be closed except for families whose sibling would be concurrently enrolled — approximately 20 students annually. Somerset Apartment students will follow their elementary cohort to middle school and then to Troy High, approximately 190 students impacted; new Somerset families enrolled during the 26/27 school year will be enrolled at Smith MS or Baker MS. Smith, Baker, and Athens will offer open enrollment.

Enrollment Adjustments: Fall 2025 actuals are Baker 621, Boulan Park 823, Larson 858, and Smith 600; Fall 2027 projections are Baker 616, Boulan Park 603, Larson 710, and Smith 597.

Timeline and assumptions: 2025/2026 prepares for adjustments and 2026/2027 implements changes. Students currently enrolled in 5th, 6th, 7th, or 8th grade (classes of 2032, 2031, 2030, and 2029) will not be impacted and may continue in their Fall 2025 building. TSD will ensure families with multiple middle-school students enrolled at the same time can keep siblings together at the same middle school. Advanced programming access, curriculum, and athletics are consistent across all four middle schools. Next steps: in September the recommendation is given to the BOE and the Board determines direction; from October through May 2026 TSD begins preparing for the recommended changes, handles logistics and communication, and monitors middle-school enrollment for further consideration.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
What it is
A memorandum dated October 2, 2025 from Shari Pawlus, Supervisor of English Language Development (ELD), K-12, to the Troy School District Board of Education. Its subject is approval of the Language Power curriculum for the district's elementary schools, and it functions as a purchase recommendation.

Background and pilot
During the 2024-25 school year, the district's elementary ELD specialists piloted Language Power across multiple sites. The pilot paired classroom use with a professional-learning plan: specialists explored the materials in focused sessions, engaged in job-embedded professional development using the curriculum in real classrooms, and received coaching from the program's teacher-developer, described as a former ELD specialist. Following the pilot, 85% of the specialists agreed that Language Power is the most effective and comprehensive resource to meet the district's multilingual learners' language-development needs.

Program description
Language Power is characterized as a research-based, standards-aligned curriculum designed specifically for multilingual learners, building academic vocabulary, reading comprehension, and writing skills through interactive lessons and scaffolded support. The program includes teacher kits with structured lesson plans, student anthologies offering leveled and engaging texts, consumable student practice workbooks, and digital access to resources. The memo notes that the mix of consumables and digital resources gives students both hands-on materials and technology-supported access, and that digital access reduces the need for annual repurchasing.

Professional learning and implementation support
Included in the quoted pricing, the vendor has agreed to provide additional professional development during the school year. This comprises an "unpacking" session to launch the materials plus ongoing job-embedded coaching/PD to support high-fidelity classroom implementation.

Funding plan
The memo proposes a two-part funding plan to implement Language Power districtwide at the elementary level:
1. Teacher Kits - $22,000, from General Funds - providing the core teacher materials needed to deliver instruction.
2. Supplemental Materials - $70,000, from Title III - including anthologies, consumable student workbooks, and digital licenses; the memo emphasizes that digital access avoids purchasing replacement materials year after year, creating a sustainable model.

Recommendation
Citing the successful pilot and strong support from specialists, Pawlus recommends that the Board approve the purchase of Language Power for elementary ELD programming, arguing it will provide multilingual learners equitable access to high-quality instruction and resources supporting academic growth and language development.

What it is
A memorandum from MJ School Policy Services (Miller Johnson) to "MJ Policy Service Clients," dated August 18, 2025, titled "Policy Manual and Administrative Regulations Update - August 2025." It transmits recommended updates and modifications to the firm's policy and administrative-regulations manuals, organized by section with individual update numbers and a narrative basis for each change. Additions are shown in red, deletions in blue, and yellow-highlighted areas require additional district-specific information.

Firm/URL note
The memo advises clients that their current online policy URL still contains the firm's prior name, "Lusk Albertson," and that the firm is working with its vendor to update this to "Miller Johnson." Updated URLs will follow, and districts are asked to update their website links to avoid service disruption. Questions may be directed to Policy@MillerJohnson.com.

The one substantive update - Personnel (4000 series)
Update 20.01 introduces a new Policy 4003, Employee Salary Schedules. Its basis is a recent Michigan Supreme Court decision, Batista v. ORS, which the memo says made clear that under the Michigan Public School Employees Retirement Act, all public-school employees must have a normal salary schedule in order to receive credit for any year-over-year increases in compensation for pension purposes. The policy is intended to ensure statutory compliance and to set out how salary schedules are created and approved. Two options are provided:
- Option 1: For districts preferring Board approval. All employees must be paid per a normal salary schedule; for employees not covered by a collective-bargaining contract that provides normal salary schedules, the District will implement schedules setting base pay for each job classification. Job classifications for non-bargaining-unit employees are determined by the Superintendent, and salary schedules for all such classifications are presented to the Board of Education for approval yearly.
- Option 2: Delegates authority to the Superintendent to create and implement normal salary schedules for all non-bargaining-unit employees (except the Superintendent), with those schedules provided to the Board prior to implementation; the Superintendent's own normal salary schedule must be presented to the Board for approval yearly.

Sections with no updates
The memo states there are no recommended updates for the Introduction (0000), Bylaws (1000), Students (2000), Curriculum and Instruction (3000), Business (5000), Facilities and Operations (6000), School and Community Relations (7000), and General Policies (8000) series. The salary-schedule policy is thus the only recommended change in this cycle.

The one substantive update - Personnel (4000 series)
Update 20.01 introduces a new Policy 4003, Employee Salary Schedules. Its basis is a recent Michigan Supreme Court decision, Batista v. ORS, which the memo says made clear that under the Michigan Public School Employees Retirement Act, all public-school employees must have a normal salary schedule in order to receive credit for any year-over-year increases in compensation for pension purposes. The policy is intended to ensure statutory compliance and to set out how salary schedules are created and approved. Two options are provided:
- Option 1: For districts preferring Board approval. All employees must be paid per a normal salary schedule; for employees not covered by a collective-bargaining contract that provides normal salary schedules, the District will implement schedules setting base pay for each job classification. Job classifications for non-bargaining-unit employees are determined by the Superintendent, and salary schedules for all such classifications are presented to the Board of Education for approval yearly.
- Option 2: Delegates authority to the Superintendent to create and implement normal salary schedules for all non-bargaining-unit employees (except the Superintendent), with those schedules provided to the Board prior to implementation; the Superintendent's own normal salary schedule must be presented to the Board for approval yearly.

The memo states there are no recommended updates for the Introduction (0000), Bylaws (1000), Students (2000), Curriculum and Instruction (3000), Business (5000), Facilities and Operations (6000), School and Community Relations (7000), and General Policies (8000) series. Scope and staffing

Trends
- Out-of-district center placements fell from 90 (2009-10) to 61, 39, and 21 (2025-26).
- ASD eligibility rose to 254 (18.6%) in 2024-25; Level 4 programs grew from 7 (2018-19) to 20 (2024-25).

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
What it is
A Special Education department update delivered at the Troy School District Board of Education workshop on October 7, 2025. Its agenda covered the Michigan Department of Education continuum of programs and services (with a focus on Least Restrictive Environment), a department overview, birth-to-age-26 service providers, special-education programming, early-childhood data, out-of-district data, disability-trend and move-in data, the Parent Advisory Committee, 2025-26 focus areas, and budget.

Continuum and caseload
Troy School District provides a full continuum of programs and services for students from birth to age 26. In 2024-25 the district served 1,367 students with Individualized Education Programs. Services span an Individual Family Service Plan (IFSP) for birth-age 3 and an Individual Education Program (IEP) for ages 3-26, with services-only supports (school social work, speech-language, teacher consultant, OT, PT) from age 3 through 12th grade, resource-room placement K-12, categorical placement from preschool to age 26, homebound services, and one Project Search program. Categorical teaching staff total 44.0 FTE.

Categorical programs
Early Childhood Special Education (ECP): 8 sections, 4 teachers; Mild Cognitive Impairments: 6 programs; Moderate Cognitive Impairments: 3; Emotional Impairments: 3; Level 3: 3; Level 4: 20 programs (15 elementary, 3 middle school, 2 high school); Troy Center for Transition: 5 programs.

Service providers (birth-26)
The ancillary team includes 26 school social workers, 22 speech-language pathologists, 10 school psychologists, 23 teacher consultants, 7 occupational therapists, 2 physical therapists, 7 Early On team members, an assistive-technology consultant, BCBA and BCaBA staff (31n grant positions), two behavior specialists, six behavior support technicians, a non-public service team, and two homebound teachers. The Special Education leadership team comprises Allison Mason (Early Childhood Coordinator), Chris Olson (IEP Quality and Compliance, SSW), Erica Conklin (Behavior Support Coordinator), Teresa Bruno (Troy Center for Transition Coordinator), and Zach Downer (Transition Coordinator). District support staff FTE include 100 para-educators/program assistants, 152 student support aides, and 11 job coaches.

Early-childhood data (birth-age 5)
Comparing 2022 to 2025: Early On (birth-3) families rose from 33 to 38; Early Childhood Program (ECP, 2 1/2-5) enrollment from 50 to 62; 1755 Program (ages 3-5, services in the natural preschool environment) from 12 to 18; itinerant speech from 59 to 54.

Out-of-district / center placements
County center-program placements - serving students with the most complex medical, physical, and behavioral needs, including Wing Lake (severe multiple impairments/SXI), Deaf and Hard of Hearing programs, and segregated programs for emotional impairments or significant autism - declined from 90 (2009-10) to 61 (2014-15), 39 (2019-20), and 21 (2025-26).

Disability eligibility and move-in trends
Of 1,367 IEPs in 2024-25: ASD eligibility grew from 121 (10.6%) in 2014-15 to 185 (14.6%) in 2020-21 to 254 (18.6%) in 2024-25; Specific Learning Disability fell from 383 (33.7%) to 289 (22.8%) to 258 (18.9%); Speech and Language Impairment moved from 307 (27%) to 417 (32.9%) to 420 (30.7%). Level 4 programming needs grew from 7 programs (2018-19) to 12 (2020-21), 15 (2022-23), and 20 (2024-25). For 2025-26, transfer students with IEPs totaled 66 currently, with 23 placed in categorical programs, 12 in Level 4 programs, and 7 new students needing immediate evaluation.

Family engagement, goals, and funding
The Special Education PAC (SSPAC) executive board members are Rebecca Gilkey, Reem Sater, and Kate Wharton, with Reem Sater serving as Oakland County PAC representative; building representatives support families and attend monthly meetings. The 2025-26 goals emphasize equitable access to high-quality instruction and inclusive practices, alignment with Teaching and Learning on MTSS and intensive intervention, evidence-based support for students with complex needs, and increased family engagement through the PAC. The presentation closes with special-education funding/budget slides and a questions slide.

- Troy Union Elementary
- Larson Middle School

- Awarded to schools that are centers of innovation, leadership, and educational excellence.
- Recognizes a clear vision for learning with technology, a culture supporting continuous innovation, and evidence of academic achievement and student engagement.
- Fewer than a thousand schools worldwide hold the distinction.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Prepared as a 'TSD Mission Moment' for the Regular Meeting of the Troy School District Board of Education on October 14, 2025, this recognition item (agenda item 2.A, dated 10.14.25) recognizes two district schools, Troy Union Elementary and Larson Middle School, for earning designation as Apple Distinguished Schools, described as one of the most prestigious honors in education.

The item explains that the Apple Distinguished School recognition is awarded to schools that are centers of innovation, leadership, and educational excellence, and that such schools demonstrate a clear vision for learning with technology, a culture that supports continuous innovation, and compelling evidence of academic achievement and student engagement. It notes that fewer than a thousand schools worldwide have earned this distinction, placing the two Troy schools among an elite group recognized by Apple for transforming teaching and learning through the thoughtful and effective use of technology. The recognition is framed as celebrating not only the use of devices but the dedication of educators, administrators, and students to leveraging technology in ways that enhance creativity, collaboration, and critical thinking.

The recommended action is to invite Mike Cottone and Brian Zawislak, the principals of the recognized schools, to come forward along with any staff members in attendance, so the Board can present the Apple Distinguished School Award and congratulate the principals, staff, and students. The item serves to publicly honor the two schools' achievement at the meeting.

What it is: Agenda item 2.B, a recognition item and resolution for the Regular Meeting of the Board of Education on October 14, 2025, commemorating October 2025 as Learning Disabilities Month in Michigan.

Context:
- National associations supporting learning differences designate October as an awareness month, including those focused on Dyslexia, ADHD, and Down Syndrome.
- The U.S. Department of Education recognizes October as Learning Disabilities / Dyslexia / ADHD / Down Syndrome Awareness Month.
- Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer has declared October as Learning Disabilities Month; the Troy Board joins in that recognition.

Resolution highlights (WHEREAS clauses):
- Learning disabilities are differences in how brains work, affecting acquisition, organization, retention, understanding, or use of verbal or nonverbal information; they range in severity and may affect oral language, reading, written language, and mathematics.
- 1 in 5 individuals has a learning disability; disabilities are a natural part of human diversity.
- Appropriate supports, assessments, and interventions help individuals achieve their goals.

Resolved: The Troy School District Board of Education joins Governor Gretchen Whitmer in commemorating October 2025 as Learning Disabilities Month in Michigan.

Recommended action: Acceptance of the resolution (with blanks for mover, supporter, and Yes/No vote).

Agenda item 2.B, dated 10.14.25, is a recognition item prepared for the Regular Meeting of the Troy School District Board of Education on October 14, 2025. It designates October 2025 as Learning Disabilities Month and presents a supporting resolution.

The introductory text explains that several national associations dedicated to supporting individuals with learning differences have designated October as a month of awareness, including organizations focused on Dyslexia, Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), and Down Syndrome. It notes that the U.S. Department of Education has recognized October as Learning Disabilities / Dyslexia / ADHD / Down Syndrome Awareness Month, and that in Michigan, Governor Whitmer has taken a broader approach by declaring October as Learning Disabilities Month. In that spirit, the Troy Board of Education wishes to join the Governor by adopting its own resolution. The recommended action is acceptance of the resolution, which includes blank lines for the mover, supporter, and Yes/No vote.

The resolution's WHEREAS clauses state that the term learning disabilities refers to differences in how brains work, which may affect the acquisition, organization, retention, understanding, or use of verbal or nonverbal information; that learning disabilities range in severity and may impact the acquisition and use of oral language, reading, written language, and mathematics; that 1 in 5 individuals has a learning disability; that learning disabilities may co-exist with other disabilities and can affect individuals regardless of race, gender, sexual orientation, or other intersecting factors; that disabilities are a natural part of human diversity though individuals may face discrimination or marginalization; that every person has strengths and learning disabilities should not keep individuals from realizing their full potential in school, at work or home, or as members of their families and communities; and that specialized assessments and interventions across home, school, community, and workplace settings can significantly enhance quality of life. The concluding clause states that the Troy School District Board of Education joins Governor Gretchen Whitmer in commemorating October 2025 as Learning Disabilities Month in Michigan.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose: Item 8.C under Business at the Troy Board of Education's October 14, 2025 Regular Meeting awards multiple technology and security bids arising from a single Request for Proposals. The RFP sought competitive bids for structured cabling, audiovisual systems, paging and emergency-notification systems, and security cameras for the new Smith Middle School. It additionally covered district-wide access-control systems, paging and emergency-notification systems for Baker Middle School, and technology work related to the Administration Building renovation. Bid responses were reviewed by Barton Malow Builders, the district's construction manager, and administration recommends the awards. The suggested resolution states: "Be it therefore resolved that the bid for technology upgrades and access controls be awarded as follows and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the 2023 Capital Projects Fund." The awards, by vendor and scope, are: Inacomp TSG for Structured Cabling at $77,464.32; VSC for PA Systems & Emergency at $719,452.00; Inacomp TSG for Classroom AV Systems at $245,974.65; People Driven Technology for Access Control at $932,248.33; People Driven Technology for Video Surveillance at $233,354.24; and People Driven Technology for a Mandatory Alternate at $244,299.00. A 10% contingency of $245,279.25 is added, bringing the TOTAL to $2,698,071.79. Thus three vendors share the work: Inacomp TSG (cabling and classroom AV), VSC (public-address and emergency systems), and People Driven Technology (access control, video surveillance, and the mandatory alternate). All of it is funded from the 2023 Capital Projects Fund, tying the spending to the district's 2023 bond program and its Smith and Baker middle school and administration-building work. The recommended action is to accept the resolution; the Moved by, Supported by, and Yes/No vote fields are left blank on the template pending the board's vote.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A memorandum from the Troy School District Finance Department dated October 2, 2025, addressed from Finance Director Aurel Malutan to Dan Trudel, Assistant Superintendent of Business Services, recommending Board approval of a cafeteria table purchase for Barnard Elementary School. The document is issued under Superintendent Dr. Richard M. Machesky and identifies the Finance Department at 4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098, with Dan Trudel as Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, and Aurel Malutan as Finance Director.

The purchase would replace the existing cafeteria tables at Barnard Elementary, which are being retired due to age and condition. The scope is 18 oval tables with bench seating around each table, intended primarily for daily lunch periods as well as before- and after-school care programs and other events and functions throughout the school year.

Pricing was obtained through the cooperative purchasing contract OCSPO AEPA-MSRP IFB-022-A and would be funded with bond funds under account number 423-016-456-0000-00-6410. Malutan recommends that School Specialty be awarded the purchase, citing its low quote for the quality level, its offering of SICO brand products under contract, and customer service that included visiting the school to measure the cafeteria so the tables would accommodate the number of students during a lunch period. School Specialty's quote includes freight with ramp delivery and installation, and the vendor absorbed SICO's price increase that took effect in January 2025.

The memo emphasizes product durability: the recommended tables are equipped with a strut system for lifting and lowering, which is expected to keep functioning over a 20-year span, whereas tables with torsion bars or springs fatigue after 7-9 years and become difficult to raise and lower. Malutan notes that this is the same brand purchased within the last three years for several other Troy School District elementary schools, specifically Bemis, Costello, Hamilton, Martell, and Troy Union, providing consistent structure and uniformity across the district. An attached revised quote and concept layout reflect $8,558 in savings from the original quote.

The recommended amount is $46,937.22 for 18 tables. Malutan requests that the letter be accepted for Board approval and provides his contact information: amalutan@troy.k12.mi.us and 248-823-4033. The purchase corresponds to the itemized School Specialty quote Q-614116 filed with the same board meeting.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A bid-award recommendation letter from Barton Malow (26500 American Dr., Southfield, MI 48034), dated October 2, 2025, addressed to Saso Vasovski, Director of Technology and Data Services at the Troy School District (4420 Livernois Rd., Troy, MI 48098), regarding Bid Package T3: Access Control and Technology Upgrades. The letter is signed by Brian Jessie, CTS, of Barton Malow, and copied to TSD's Alan Wilson, BMB's Josh Eisenman, and Lecole Planners' Michelle Kerns.

Bid Package T3 was released on July 7, 2025 and includes five bid categories - structured cabling, audiovisual systems, paging and emergency notification systems, and security cameras for the new Smith Middle School - plus district-wide access control systems, paging and emergency notification for Baker Middle School, and technology work related to the Administration Building renovation. A non-mandatory prebid meeting was held virtually on July 16, 2025. Twenty-seven bids were received and publicly opened on August 12, 2025. Barton Malow and the Troy School District technology team confirmed the proposals met scope and schedule, conducted bidder interviews, and evaluated solutions through vendor demonstrations.

The recommended awards are: bid 27-1 (structured cabling) to Inacomp TSG for $77,464.32; bid 27-2 (IP public address and emergency notification) to VSC, Inc. for $719,452.00; bid 27-3 (classroom AV systems) to Inacomp TSG for $245,974.65; bid 28-1 (access control) to People Driven Technology for $932,248.33; and bid 28-2 (video surveillance) to People Driven Technology for a base bid of $233,354.24 plus a mandatory alternate of $244,299.00. The total amount of contracts is $2,452,792.54, a 10% contingency adds $245,279.25, and the grand total project award is $2,698,071.79.

The attached bid tabulation lists all bidders. For 27-1 structured cabling, bids ranged from Division 27, LLC at $67,780.76 (low) through Inacomp TSG $77,464.32, National Systems Installers $84,550.00, Propel Tech & Electric $91,853.10, Nerds Xpress $93,020.79, SSD Cabling Cameras $95,529.18, AMcomm $101,250.00, Technology Solutions Unlimited $104,677.00, and Allcomm (incomplete) $202,665.60. For 27-2, Inacomp TSG bid $672,203.80 and VSC $719,452.00. For 27-3, Inacomp TSG bid $245,974.65 and TEL Systems $250,469.41. For 28-1 access control, bidders included Fontanesi & Kann $711,458.00, People Driven Technology $932,248.33, Mobile Communications America $943,691.18, Technology Install Partners $999,464.00, and Parkway Electric & Communications $1,022,451.00. For 28-2 video surveillance, bidders included Mobile Communications America, AMcomm, Metro Detroit Integrated Systems, Fontanesi & Kann, People Driven Technology ($233,354.24 base / $244,299.00 alternate), and Parkway Electric.

The letter notes that People Driven Technology is the low bidder offering the Genetec solution, which manages video security cameras and access-controlled doors under a unified software platform with third-party integrations, so that both access control and video security will be unified under a single district-wide software solution. VSC is noted as currently completing similar work at 10 elementary buildings in the district.
